name: Lokrum
label: Lokrum Island
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Buža Bar' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Buža Bar' (node/897464872): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/6193666: large area 'Lokrum' (1836 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Forested island just off the Old Town, reached by boat.

text.description: Lokrum is a small wooded island just off Dubrovnik, about 600 metres from the city, stretching from north-west to south-east. It photographs well because it gives the sea view a calm, green shape on the horizon, set against the pale stone of the Old Town. This spot is a cliff-side view of it, so you are photographing the island from the mainland rather than on it. The island has a long story. A Benedictine abbey was founded there in 1023, and in 1859 Archduke Maximilian had a mansion and garden laid out. Fort Royal, built under French rule, stands on the highest point, 96 metres above the sea. Peacocks brought over by Maximilian still live on the island. For a phone photo, aim to place Lokrum on one of the gridline thirds with plenty of sea and sky around it. That makes the island feel properly distant and gives the picture a calm, simple shape. If you also want a layered coastal view, Banje Beach shows Lokrum between the beach and the Old Town walls. Bernarda Shawa looks south over the roofs and walls towards the island.
text.geographic_location: On the cliffs just outside the south wall of Dubrovnik's Old Town, facing the sea. Lokrum lies across the water to the south-east.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Old Town. Buža Bar is reached through a small doorway in the south wall, which leads out onto the cliff terrace. Once there, face south-east and Lokrum is across the water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the island with the open sea around it. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Lokrum closer and fill more of the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the cliff edge and a lot of sky in the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Buža Bar (cliff terrace outside the city wall, looking out over the sea). Lokrum sitting on the horizon over open water, with the city wall behind the photographer. Face south-east towards the island.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line, with Lokrum on one of the side thirds. Keep the sea in the foreground so the island has room. If you want a different angle, Banje Beach shows Lokrum between the beach and the Old Town walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the island to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky and sea stay rich rather than washed out. Hold the phone steady with both hands when you zoom in, as the island is far away and any shake will show.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when guides mention golden light. Buža Bar is open only in spring and summer, so check this before you go.

text.access_note: Access to the Buža Bar terrace is free, but you may need to buy a drink to get a seat, so check the official site before you go. Lokrum itself is a nature reserve reached by ferry from the Old City port.
claims_not_in_sources: At sunset the sun is low in the west, so from this terrace facing south-east the light falls from behind and to one side.
The island will look small at the default lens (1x), so the telephoto lens is useful if your phone has one.
Not every phone has a telephoto lens; the zoom range of 2x-5x depends on the model.

name: Walls of Dubrovnik
label: City Walls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Skalini Dr. Marka Foteza' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Skalini Doktor Marka Foteza' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2294262: large area 'Walls of Dubrovnik' (911 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The famous medieval walls encircling the Old Town, best walked at the start or end of the day.

text.description: Dubrovnik's city walls wrap around most of the Old Town in one unbroken stone circuit of about 1,940 metres, rising to roughly 25 metres at their highest. Most of what you see was built between the 13th and 17th centuries. Towers, bastions and forts break up the line, and the walls were added to UNESCO's World Heritage list together with the Old Town in 1979. For a phone photo, the best view is from outside and below. From these steps the pale stone, the terracotta roofs behind it and the West Harbour all fit into one frame, and you don't need a walls ticket to stand there. The steps also give you a natural foreground: the handrail, the stone treads or a bit of greenery help lead the eye towards the walls. Inside the walls you get the rooftop views, but you can't see the walls themselves, so this outside angle shows their scale much better. If you want a rooftop panorama as well, Tvrđava Minčeta looks over the Old Town roofs and the sea, and Iza Grada frames the walls from outside the ramparts. The walls are very busy in summer, so expect other people on the steps too.
text.geographic_location: On the western side of Dubrovnik's Old Town, outside the walls on the path up to Fort Lovrijenac, close to the West Harbour. The walls themselves circle the Old Town.
text.directions_text: Walk the last part from the Pile Gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the walls, the roofs and the harbour into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out a single tower or a stretch of wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Skalini Dr. Marka Foteza (stairs on the climb up to Fort Lovrijenac, outside the walls). The walls and Old Town seen from outside and below, with the West Harbour in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the line of the walls along the lower or upper third, leaving the harbour on one side. Use a step or handrail in the foreground to add depth. Take a few shots from different steps, because each one changes how much of the harbour you see. For a rooftop panorama as an alternative, Tvrđava Minčeta is recommended for its view over the Old Town and the sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the walls to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone and the sky keep their detail. Keep the phone steady against the handrail. Panorama mode can work along a wide stretch of the harbour, but wait for people to pass before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon is usually calmer and has softer light. Midday in summer is the busiest and the harshest.

text.access_note: The stairs are outside the ticketed walls circuit, but walking the walls themselves needs a ticket and the walls close before sunset, so check the official site before you go, including whether Fort Lovrijenac is covered.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or later afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people than midday in summer.
The steps may be used by other visitors heading up to Fort Lovrijenac, so they can be busy.
Slightly lowering the exposure helps keep detail in pale stone against a bright sky.
A handrail or step in the foreground can add depth to the photo.

name: Banje Beach
label: Banje Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Frana Supila' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Frana Supila nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W171254027 (Banje): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: City beach with a view of the walls and Lokrum.

text.description: Banje is Dubrovnik's pebble beach just outside the Old Town, and it photographs well because the view has layers. Sea and beach sit in the foreground, the Old Town stands behind them, and Lokrum Island closes the frame. The best-known angle is from the street above, at the top of the stairs down to the beach. From there you look down onto the pebbles and the water, which gives the picture depth and keeps other people's heads out of the foreground. Photo guides treat this raised spot as the classic one, and it is the easiest to reach on foot from the Old Town. The views from above are good all along the beach, so you can walk a little to either side and try a slightly different angle. Be aware that the beach has paid sunbed and bar areas, and the free strip is narrow. In July and August it is crowded with cruise day-trippers, so early morning is the calmest time for a clean shot. In winter the sunbeds and bars are removed, which gives a tidier picture. Take a wide shot first to show the whole scene, then a closer one picking out the Old Town or Lokrum. Check that the edges of your frame are straight, because the sea gives you a clear horizon to line up against.
text.geographic_location: Banje Beach is on the edge of the Old Town in Dubrovnik. The viewpoint is on the street Frana Supila, above the beach.
text.directions_text: The viewpoint is on the street Frana Supila, at the top of the stairs that lead down to Banje Beach, and it is the easiest viewpoint to reach from the Old Town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view down onto the beach. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole beach, the Old Town and Lokrum in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Lokrum Island or the Old Town walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Frana Supila (at the top of the stairs down to the beach). A raised angle looking down onto the pebble beach, with the Old Town and Lokrum Island behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, with the beach filling the lower part of the frame. Let the Old Town and Lokrum sit in the background. For a different view, a low angle from the beach at the east end looks along white rock formations towards the Old Town. The rocks may be slippery, so take care.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the beach or the Old Town to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sea and sky keep their colour. Take a few shots in case someone walks through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the least crowded time, especially in July and August. Winter is cleaner for photos because the beach concessions are removed.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is on a public street, but the beach below has paid sunbed and bar areas.

name: St Blaise's Church
label: St Blaise's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stradun' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Stradun nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1297393787: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Blaise's Church' (39 m across).
notes: Baroque church dedicated to the city's patron saint.

text.description:
St Blaise's Church is the Baroque church dedicated to the patron saint of Dubrovnik, once the protector of the independent Republic of Ragusa. The building you see today dates from 1715. The Venetian architect and sculptor Marino Gropelli built it on the foundations of the medieval church, which burned down in 1706. The facade is easy to read in a phone photo: a flight of steps leads up to the portal, four Corinthian columns divide the front, and a semicircular gable carries a balustrade topped with three statues. A free-standing Saint Blaise stands in the middle, with Faith and Hope either side. Behind the facade is an oblong dome.

The church photographs best from Stradun, the long limestone street. From its west end the street leads the eye straight to the church front, with the facade and dome framed head-on. For a second option, Luža Square puts the Orlando Column in front of the facade, so you get two landmarks in one frame. Ploče Gate shows the church against the city walls, which makes a less usual backdrop.

Luža Square is very crowded at midday and during the 3 February Feast of St Blaise procession, so allow extra time or aim for a quieter hour. Photography is discouraged inside the church, and flash is generally discouraged too, so keep your best shots for the outside.
text.geographic_location: St Blaise's Church stands in the heart of Dubrovnik's Old Town, at the far end of Stradun beside Luža Square.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby, so simply walk to the west end of Stradun in Dubrovnik's Old Town. Walk east along the street and it will be in front of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole street leading to the church. Then try 2x or 3x telephoto, if your phone has it, to bring the facade and dome closer and make the street look more compressed. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only on Luža Square, where you want the column and the church together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Stradun (west end of the street, looking east toward the church). The church sits centred at the far end of the long limestone street, with its facade and dome framed straight on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the church on the centre line, so the street's edges lead into it. Keep the phone level so the buildings along the street don't lean. If you want something different, Luža Square gives a two-landmark shot with the Orlando Column in front of the facade. Ploče Gate shows the church against the city walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the pale stone looks washed out. Wait for a gap in the crowd and take a few frames, or try a Live Photo to choose the cleanest moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the street is quieter. Avoid midday and the 3 February procession if you want an uncrowded frame. Check how the light falls on the facade on the day and adjust your timing to suit.

text.access_note: The church is a working place of worship where photography inside is discouraged, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
claims_not_in_sources: Stradun and Luža Square are in Dubrovnik's Old Town.
Early morning is typically quieter on Stradun than midday.
There are no train stations or tram stops near the spot.

name: Pile Gate
label: Pile Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dubrovačke Gradske Zidine' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Gradske zidine' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OSM W668283215 (Pile Gate): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The main western entrance to the Old Town.

text.description: Pile Gate is a western entrance to Dubrovnik's old town, and it works as a photo stop in two ways. From the wall walk above it, you look down Stradun, the limestone street lined with pale facades. From outside, you can photograph the gate itself with its stone bridge approach and the outer fortifications around the entrance. Guides often say the wall walk gives a better Stradun picture than shooting from street level. The Franciscan dome sometimes sits in the corner of the view, which adds a landmark and a bit of depth. The gate area is busy for most of the day, so people will usually be in your frame. Allow for that: use them as scale in the street view, or go early. There may also be roadworks or bus activity near the gate that affect the foreground, so take a quick look before you pick your angle. For a different picture, Pile Bay on the harbour side shows the old town and the city walls with a pier in the foreground. Local names for that spot vary, so check the label on the map. Whichever angle you choose, keep your phone lens clean, since a smear catches the sun on pale stone, and take several frames in case someone walks across.
text.geographic_location: Pile Gate sits on the western edge of Dubrovnik's old town, at the point where the city walls meet the approach from outside. Stradun, the old town's main street, begins just inside it.
text.directions_text: There is no nearby station or tram stop for this spot, though a bus terminal may be near the gate. If you are going up onto the walls, remember that the wall walk needs a paid walls ticket. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the Stradun view from the walls; it keeps the street and facades looking natural. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the gate and its bridge approach if you are standing close. Try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the Franciscan dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the wall walk directly above the gate, looking down Stradun). A straight-down view of Stradun's limestone street and facades, with the Franciscan dome sometimes framing the corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the centre of Stradun up with a vertical line, so the street runs away from you evenly. Include a little of the wall edge in a lower corner for depth. If you also want the full gate with its stone bridge and outer fortifications, take that from outside the gate, or try Pile Bay for the walls seen from the harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale street to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the stone does not turn white. Take a few frames in a row, because the crowds change the scene from one second to the next.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides advise getting there early in the morning, at opening, before the crowds arrive.

text.access_note: The wall walk above the gate needs a paid walls ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Stradun
label: Stradun
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vrata od Pila (Pile Gate)' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Vrata od Pila' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1818100: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The limestone-paved main street of the Old Town.

text.description: Stradun is the main street of Dubrovnik's Old Town, a limestone-paved pedestrian street about 300 metres long, running from Pile Gate in the west to Ploče Gate in the east. The ground was once a marshy channel, reclaimed in the 13th century, and the street became the city's main thoroughfare soon after. Most of what you see today dates from after the 1667 earthquake. Afterwards the Republic of Ragusa set rules for how houses were built, so the buildings along the street share the same pattern: a shop at ground level under a rounded arch, with living rooms above. That sameness is why it photographs so well. The rows of matching frontages lead the eye along a pale, polished street, with bell towers and fountains at each end. The street becomes a bright line between the rooftops, with a neat, symmetrical feel. For a cleaner picture, try early morning or after dark, when the street is emptier. Shell damage from the 1991–92 siege has mostly been repaired. Once you have the view from above, walk down for a second shot from Luža Square, looking west along the street, or from Onofrio's Fountain, with the street and the Franciscan church behind it.
text.geographic_location: Stradun runs east–west through the middle of Dubrovnik's walled Old Town. It links Pile Gate on the western side with Ploče Gate and the Bell Tower area at the eastern end.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops serve this spot, so the Old Town is reached on foot, heading for Pile Gate. The street lies about 100 metres to the east of it. You can also simply walk in through Pile Gate and follow the street east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-down view of the street. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the rooftops and the far end of the street. The ultra-wide (0.5x) takes in more of the gate and walls, but it can stretch the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Vrata od Pila (Pile Gate) (elevated section of the city walls just above the gate stairs, looking down the street). A straight-down, symmetrical view of Stradun from above, with the limestone street as a bright line between the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the street along the centre line so both rows of rooftops balance. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a different angle, try Luža Square, looking west along the full length of the street, or Onofrio's Fountain, with the fountain in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the street to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pale stone does not wash out. Use night mode after dark, resting your elbows on the wall to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or after dark, when the street is empty. Good light also brings out the sheen on the stone. Check the official site for the walls' opening times.

text.access_note: The street itself is pedestrian-only, but the city walls above Pile Gate need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Rector's Palace
label: Rector's Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Luža' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Luža' (way/171861541): middle (53 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5861269: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Knežev dvor' (51 m across).
notes: Gothic-Renaissance palace of the former Republic of Ragusa.

text.description:
The Rector's Palace was the seat of government for the Republic of Ragusa, the old city-state of Dubrovnik. The palace was the seat of the Rector of the Republic of Ragusa from the 14th century until 1808. The building is mostly Gothic, with Renaissance and Baroque touches, and you can see the mix in the arcade along the front. The palace has a turbulent past. A fire in 1435 led to a rebuild, a gunpowder explosion in 1463 did serious damage, and the earthquake of 1667 brought more repairs, this time in Baroque style. Since 1872 part of it has housed the history department of the Museum of Dubrovnik.

For photographs, the best view is from Luža, the square that the palace faces. From there the arched facade fills the frame, and behind it you can pick up the Cathedral and other Old Town buildings. The row of arches also works as a natural frame. Stand back far enough to keep the whole front in view, then step in for a second shot of a single arch or a carved capital. Walking along the Stradun towards Luža, the palace comes into view at the far end. In the evening the palace is lit up, which makes the facade stand out.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Dubrovnik, on the side of the square called Luža. The palace faces the square and stands close to the Cathedral.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby, so make your way to the Old Town on foot and walk along the Stradun to Luža. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the arches won't all fit. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for single arches, capitals and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Luža (from the square, facing the palace's arched facade). The palace's arched Gothic-Renaissance facade filling the frame across the square, with the Cathedral and nearby Old Town buildings in the background. Face the palace's arched front, which lies to the south-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines, so the arches look straight. Keep the whole facade in view, with the Cathedral behind it. For a second shot, go closer and frame one arch with the shaded arcade behind it. If you walk down the Stradun first, you can also take a shot of the palace appearing at the far end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit stone is not washed out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone still against your body or a solid ledge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening or night, when the palace is lit up. Sunset is also a good time.

text.access_note: Luža is an open public square, but the palace interior is a ticketed museum, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The palace is about 1 minute on foot from the stand-here point (72 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
Walking along the Stradun towards Luža, the palace comes into view at the far end (from the viewpoint notes).
Stepping back, using the ultra-wide, using gridlines and lowering the exposure are general phone techniques and not specific to this site.

name: Fort Lovrijenac
label: Fort Lovrijenac
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Park Gradac' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Park Gradac' (way/1322303615): middle (301 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/165354386: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Lovrijenac' (72 m across).
notes: The rock-top fortress known as Dubrovnik's Gibraltar.

text.description:
Lovrijenac, also called St Lawrence Fortress, stands on a rocky headland just outside the western wall of Dubrovnik. It sits about 37 metres above the sea and has long been nicknamed "Dubrovnik's Gibraltar". The fort has a triangular plan with three terraces. Its outer walls are up to 12 metres thick, while the walls facing the city are only about 60 centimetres thick. Above the gate is the Latin inscription Non Bene Pro Toto Libertas Venditur Auro: liberty cannot be sold for all the gold in the world. The chronicles say the people of Dubrovnik built it in just three months to stop Venice getting there first. Today it is also a stage, and Hamlet performed here is a symbol of the Dubrovnik Summer Festival.

It photographs well because the pale stone seems to grow straight out of the cliff, with the sea around it. A good, quieter angle is from across the bay at Park Gradac, which gives a clear, unobstructed view of the fort with the sea and the Old Town walls behind it, and it is usually quieter than the busy spots by the walls. If you have time, the West Harbour and Fort Bokar give other angles on the fort. Whichever you choose, keep the fort in the left or right third of the frame and leave room for the water.
text.geographic_location: Lovrijenac is just outside the western wall of Dubrovnik's Old Town, on a rock beside the small bay on that side of the walls. Park Gradac, the viewing spot, lies across that bay from the fort.
text.directions_text: Head to Park Gradac, which is across the bay from the fortress. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the fort, the bay and the Old Town walls together. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the fortress closer and pick out its terraces and gate. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky, as the fort will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Park Gradac (viewpoint across the bay from the fortress). The fortress seen across the bay, with the sea and the Old Town walls in the background. From here the fort is to the south-east, with the sea and the Old Town walls behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the fort on one of the vertical lines, with the water filling the lower part of the frame and the Old Town walls behind. Take one wide shot at 1x, then a closer one with the telephoto. If you also visit the West Harbour or Fort Bokar, you will get the fort rising from the cliff or framed by the western walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fort to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail and the sky stays colourful. Hold the phone steady with both hands, resting your elbows on a wall or railing if you can.

text.access_note: Park Gradac is an open public space, but walking the City Walls and entering the fort both need tickets, so check the official site before you go for prices and opening hours.
claims_not_in_sources: The Old Town walls are visible behind the fort from Park Gradac, and the fort's pale stone can lose detail in bright light.
Resting your elbows on a wall or railing helps keep a phone steady.

name: Sponza Palace
label: Sponza Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Placa' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Placa nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2301265: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palača Sponza' (52 m across).

text.description: Sponza Palace stands at the eastern end of Stradun, Dubrovnik's long limestone main street. It works well for photos because the street leads the eye straight to it, and the arches frame the view along the street. The palace was built between 1516 and 1522 in a mix of Gothic and Renaissance styles, and the loggia and its carvings are the work of the Andrijić brothers and other stonecutters. Over the centuries it has been a customs house, mint, armoury, treasury, bank and school. It came through the 1667 earthquake undamaged. Today it houses the Dubrovnik State Archive, whose records go back to the 12th century. A Latin inscription about honest weights and measures is carved on an arch inside. The best view is from Placa, the local name for Stradun, looking back at the palace. If you want the facade with its Renaissance portico, the Clock Tower beside it and the Orlando Column in front, try Luža Square instead. For a quieter picture, the inner courtyard has arches and columns that frame the stonework. Before you go, bear in mind that one reviewer reported the facade was under restoration, which can block the view. The courtyard may also be taken up by art exhibitions.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Dubrovnik, at the eastern end of Stradun, on Luža Square next to the Clock Tower.
text.directions_text: Head to the Old Town of Dubrovnik, then walk along Stradun towards its eastern end, where the palace stands. Look north from there and the palace is straight ahead. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the palace sits at the end of the street with the Stradun paving leading towards it. Use the telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the loggia and carvings. If you step into the courtyard, the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit in the arches and columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Placa (east end of Stradun, looking back toward the palace). The palace framed at the end of the Stradun's long limestone street, with the arches giving a view along the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the street up with the centre of the frame, so the paving acts as a leading line to the palace. Keep the phone level so the building edges stay straight. For a different angle, try Luža Square, with the Orlando Column in the foreground and the Clock Tower beside the palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the pale stone looks washed out. Take a few shots in a row, because people keep walking through the frame. Don't use portrait mode here, as it is meant for people and works poorly on buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the evening, when Stradun is usually quieter and easier to photograph without crowds.

text.access_note: Stradun and Luža Square are open public space, but the palace interior, courtyard and archive may have restricted access or varying hours, so check the official site before you go. Drones are not permitted in the Old Town, and the memorial room inside calls for discreet photography.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late evening are usually quieter on Stradun.
Pedestrians walking through the frame are likely at busy times of day.
Portrait mode is designed for people and works poorly on buildings.

name: Mount Srđ
label: Srđ viewpoint
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1609295113: the OpenStreetMap point 'Srđ'.
notes: The hilltop above the Old Town with the classic panorama, reached by cable car.

text.description:
Srđ is the low mountain directly behind Dubrovnik's walled city, and it is the place to go when you want the whole picture in one frame. It rises to 412 metres, and from the top you can see the Old Town, Lokrum island, the Adriatic and the line of the Stradun. A large white stone cross stands at the summit, next to Fort Imperial, a defensive building put up by the French in 1810 during the Napoleonic Wars. The fort now houses a museum about the Croatian War of Independence (1991–1995), and Srđ was a centre of fierce fighting during the Siege of Dubrovnik. That history gives the view some weight beyond the red roofs.

It photographs well because of the height. The terracotta roofs, the city walls and the sea sit in layers below you, so a simple phone shot already looks composed. The cross and the fort walls also give you a foreground to put against the city. Stand a little back from any edge, turn on gridlines and place the horizon on a top or bottom line. Try one wide shot of the whole scene, then a closer one of a single detail such as the Stradun or Lokrum. The cable car has reopened and there is a restaurant at the top. A long, steep footpath also climbs from the town through pine trees, so allow time and take water.
text.geographic_location: Srđ is the mountain immediately behind the walled Old Town of Dubrovnik, rising above the city, with the fort and white cross at its top.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground-style stops are listed for this spot, so start from the walled Old Town, which lies just below Srđ. From there the mountain rises just behind the city, and you can reach the top by the cable car or on the long, steep footpath that climbs through the pines. Check the official cable car site before you go for running times and access. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of city, sea and island with the cross or fort wall in the foreground. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the Old Town and the coast. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Stradun, the rooftops or Lokrum.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face towards the walled city and the sea below and keep the cross or a fort wall at the edge of the frame for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom third line. Keep the walled city in the lower half and let the sea and sky fill the rest. Use a fort wall or the cross as a foreground edge, and hold the phone level so the horizon stays straight. For a wide view, try panorama mode and move slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Old Town to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the roofs are not washed out. Use panorama for the full sweep of coast, and night mode at dusk if the city lights are on, resting your elbows on a wall to stay steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening usually gives softer light and warmer colours on the city and sea. Midday often looks flatter and hazier.

text.access_note: The summit has a fort with a museum, a restaurant and a cable car, so check the official site before you go for access, opening and any tickets.

name: Franciscan Friary
label: Franciscan Friary
camera_source: Commons cluster (6 photos), weak. Moved 26 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 20 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/843131885: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Francis Church' (59 m across).
notes: Cloister and old pharmacy beside Pile Gate on Stradun.

text.description: The Franciscan friary and church stands on Stradun, Dubrovnik's main street, right by the Pile Gate end of the old town. The complex holds a church, a friary with two cloisters, a library and a pharmacy. For a phone photo, the church portal is the part to aim for. The earthquake of 1667 destroyed the church, and the portal is the only part that survived. It was carved in 1498 in the Gothic style by the workshop of the brothers Leonard and Petar Petrović. Look for the Pietà in the central lunette, with St Jerome and St John the Baptist on either side and the figure of the Father Creator on top. The friary pharmacy dates from 1317 and is described as the oldest still-working pharmacy in Europe. The lower cloister has 120 columns, and the carved capitals are all different. The poet Ivan Gundulić is buried in the church. The stone facade and the busy street in front make a good scene with a lot going on. Use the gridlines and keep the phone level so the portal and the vertical lines stay straight. Start with a wide view that shows the building in its street, then move in on the carved detail. People will often walk through your frame, so take a few shots and pick the best.
text.geographic_location: In the old town of Dubrovnik, on Stradun (also called the Placa), close to the Pile Gate. The church portal overlooks the start of the main street.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so it is best reached on foot from the Pile Gate, close to the friary. Walk onto Stradun and you will see the church portal beside the start of the street. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and portal. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the whole front in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Pietà and the carved figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the portal on one of the vertical lines. Keep the phone upright and level, so the building doesn't lean. Take one wide shot with some of Stradun in it, then a closer one of the lunette with the Pietà.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone of the portal to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or bright paving is washing out the carving. At 0.5x, stay clear of the edges of the frame, because buildings can stretch there.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning or in the evening, when there are fewer people on Stradun. Check which way the facade is lit on the day you go, as strong direct sun can make the carving harsh.

text.access_note: The street outside is open public space, but the church, cloisters, library and museum may be ticketed or have visiting rules and a dress code, so check the official site before you go.

name: Dubrovnik Cathedral
label: Dubrovnik Cathedral
camera_source: Commons cluster (2 photos), weak. Moved 3 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 15 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/737699509: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Assumption Cathedral' (50 m across).
notes: Baroque cathedral of the Assumption of the Virgin.

text.description:
Dubrovnik Cathedral, also called the Cathedral of the Assumption, is the Roman Catholic cathedral of the city. It is a Baroque building, and the main reason to photograph it is its façade and its large dome. The façade has a doorway flanked by four Corinthian columns, with a big Baroque window and gable above and statues of saints along the balustrade. Deep niches hold statues of Saint Blaise, the city's patron saint, and of Joseph with the Child.

The present cathedral replaced earlier churches that the 1667 earthquake destroyed. Work began in 1671, went on in stages for about four decades, and was finished in 1713. The design is traditionally credited to the Roman architect Andrea Buffalini. Inside, the main altar holds a triptych attributed to Titian. The cathedral is also part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for Dubrovnik. An earlier Byzantine basilica lies beneath it, and the English king Richard the Lionheart is said to have helped pay for an early church here after surviving a shipwreck in 1192.

For photos, think in terms of the whole building and then the details. Take a wide shot first to get the façade and the dome together, then move closer for the columns and statues. The side walls are rather plain, so the façade and dome make the better pictures. Wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground, and keep your phone straight so the vertical lines stay upright.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in Dubrovnik, Croatia.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so find the spot on the map and walk there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the façade and the dome in one frame, since you are close to a large building. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues in the niches and the top of the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Poljana Luža (west side of the square, looking across at the cathedral). The cathedral's Baroque front seen across the square at a slight angle, with St Blaise's Church and Orlando's Column nearby. Stay at this spot for your first shots, then step a little closer or to one side if people are in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the building with them so the walls do not lean. Keep the dome in the top part of the frame. For a detail shot, use zoom on the four columns and the statues rather than walking right up to them. Take a second frame with a few people in the foreground to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the detail in the stone is not lost. Hold the phone with both hands and take two or three shots in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. The middle of a sunny day can make the light harsh and the crowds thicker.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a place of worship, so expect modest dress, and check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements, including the treasury.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people than midday.
A place of worship usually expects modest dress.
The side walls are plainer, so the façade and dome make better pictures.

name: Minčeta Tower
label: Minčeta Tower
pin_note: Position from OSM W172454061 (Tower Minčeta): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The highest point of the city walls with sweeping views.

text.description:
Minčeta Tower in Dubrovnik makes a strong, solid shape against the sky. Its heavy round form is easy to pick out, so it works well as the main subject of a photo. It also gives a sense of scale if you include a little of the sky and the surroundings.

This is close enough to see the stonework, but far enough to fit the whole tower in the frame without tilting your phone up sharply. Tilting up makes the tower lean inwards, so try to hold the phone level and let the tower sit in the middle of the frame.

Turn on the gridlines in your camera settings and line the tower up with one of the vertical lines. If other visitors pass through the frame, wait a moment for a gap, or include one or two people deliberately to show scale. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then a closer one with the zoom for the detail of the stone.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole tower in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the stonework. Only use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want a lot of sky and surroundings, and keep the tower away from the edges, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pile Gate bridge (approach to Pile Gate, outside the walls, with Mount Srđ behind). The tower's rounded crown and upper walls seen from below and outside, with Mount Srđ rising behind it. The tower should sit in front of you, to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the phone level so the tower stays upright. Put the tower on one of the grid lines rather than dead centre if you want to leave room for the sky. Take a wide shot first, then a closer one.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Stone usually keeps its detail better in a slightly darker picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: Check local access information before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The tower has a round shape that stands out against the sky.
Access to the tower can be restricted, so it is worth checking local information.

name: Onofrio's Fountain
label: Onofrio's Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Poljana Paska Miličevića' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Poljana Paska Miličevića' (relation/11567772): middle (67 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N4306027796 (Onofrio's fountain): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The 16-sided Renaissance fountain just inside Pile Gate.

text.description:
Onofrio's Fountain is the large round fountain just inside Pile Gate. It photographs well because it is a clear, sculptural shape with a lively scene around it: the gate behind, the Stradun running ahead, and people passing all day. The fountain has a 16-sided form, and carved stone masks with water spouts run around it, so you can shoot it both wide and close.

For the classic picture, stand in the square just inside the gate and step back until you see the fountain's whole curve with the Old Town entrance and Pile Gate behind it. For a second angle, walk onto the Stradun and shoot back with the fountain in the foreground, the Holy Saviour Church beside it and the stone paving leading away. Then move in close for the masks and the water. Note that some spouts may not be running, so check what is flowing before you plan a close-up.

This is a busy corner at peak hours, so go early if you want a clear frame. The Stradun's limestone can be slippery when wet, so take care where you plant your feet. This is the large fountain; the small Onofrio's Fountain near Luža Square is a different structure.
text.geographic_location: In Dubrovnik's Old Town, just inside Pile Gate, with the Stradun leading on from it and the Holy Saviour Church close by.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot; head on foot to Pile Gate. The fountain is about 21 m to the north, a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole fountain with the gate behind it, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved masks and water spouts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Poljana Paska Miličevića (just inside Pile Gate, facing back toward the fountain). A wide shot of the round fountain with the Old Town entrance and Pile Gate context behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Step back until the fountain's full curve sits inside the gateway approach, and turn on gridlines to keep the edges straight. For a different view, walk onto the Stradun and put the fountain in the foreground with the Holy Saviour Church and the paving behind it. Move close for the masks and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the bright stone and water keep their detail. At blue hour, use night mode and rest your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady. Live Photos can catch the moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is least crowded. Blue hour on the Stradun also suits a long-exposure look.

text.access_note: The viewpoint square and the fountain are in the open Old Town, but check the official site before you go if you plan to combine this with any ticketed sights nearby.

name: Franjo Tuđman Bridge
label: Tuđman Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Obala Ivana Pavla II.' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Obala pape Ivana Pavla II.' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/319547414: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Most dr. Franja Tuđmana' (496 m across).
notes: Cable-stayed bridge over the Rijeka Dubrovačka inlet.

text.description: The Franjo Tuđman Bridge is the large cable-stayed bridge that carries the D8 road across Rijeka Dubrovačka, the inlet beside Gruž harbour, on the western approach to Dubrovnik. Its A-shaped pylon stands 141.5 metres tall, with 38 cable stays fanning out to the deck. The bridge is 518 metres long and was officially opened on 21 May 2002. The name was changed to the Franjo Tuđman Bridge in 2004, though the plate on the pillar still reads "Most Dubrovnik". It photographs well because its shapes are so clean: the tall pylon, the sweep of the cables and the long, thin deck across the water. From there you get a close, low-angle view up at the underside and the span, which is very different from the usual distant views. Tilt the phone upwards and let the cables lead the eye to the top of the pylon. If you want the bridge as part of a wider scene, there are two other places to try: Vidikovac Lozica for a panorama with Dubrovnik and the coast behind, and Mandrac Beach Pier for a view from the water's edge. This is a working road bridge, so keep clear of traffic and stay on the quay.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses Rijeka Dubrovačka near the Port of Gruž, on the western approach to Dubrovnik.
text.directions_text: Head for the Gruž harbour area and the bus station quay. Look for Obala Ivana Pavla II. beside the bus station, then walk a short way along the quay until you are under the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the pylon, the cables and the deck all fit in one frame from underneath. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the span. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the top of the pylon or the pattern of the cables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Obala Ivana Pavla II. (quay near the bus station, where you stand directly under the bridge). A close, low-angle view up at the bridge's underside and span from the quay.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and tilt the phone up, placing the pylon on one of the vertical lines so the cables fan out diagonally across the frame. Try a second shot with the deck running across the top as a strong horizontal. For an alternative with more surroundings, Vidikovac Lozica gives a panorama with Dubrovnik and the coast behind the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the structure does not wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something solid so the lights stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or around sunset usually gives softer light on the structure. After dark the bridge is lit up, which makes a good night-mode shot.

text.access_note: Pedestrian access onto the bridge deck is unclear, so check on the ground and at the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or around sunset usually gives softer light on the bridge.

name: Fort Bokar
label: Fort Bokar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dubrovnik City Walls' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'City Walls Hostel' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OSM W172456340 (Bokar): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Round fortress guarding the Pile Gate approach, with views of Lovrijenac.

text.description: Fort Bokar is the rounded fort on the sea side of Dubrovnik's city walls, close to Pile Bay and with Fort Lovrijenac standing out on its rock beyond. It photographs well because its curved seaward side gives a strong shape against open water, and the cliffs and sea behind it keep the frame uncluttered. One common angle is from the harbour side at Pile Bay, looking across the small inlet to the fort rising from the rocks. The exact stand point there is not fixed, so check the map. From there Bokar sits in profile to one side of the frame, with the sea and Lovrijenac in the distance. That second view needs a wall-walk ticket, so check the official site before you go. Guides suggest early morning or late afternoon, when it is less crowded, and summer crowds can be heavy. On a phone, keep the fort off-centre and let the sea fill the other half. Hold the phone steady against the wall, take two or three frames, and choose the one with no heads in the corner. If you only have time for one view, the wall walk gives a calmer composition. Pile Bay shows the fort's rounded seaward profile with Lovrijenac beyond.
text.geographic_location: On the western side of Dubrovnik's Old Town, where the city walls meet the sea near Pile Bay. Fort Lovrijenac is visible across the water beyond it.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so it is reached on foot. From there, face north-west to look back at the fort. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the fort, the sea and Lovrijenac together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Lovrijenac closer behind the fort. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the whole rounded wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (south wall, a short walk past the fort, looking back at it). Bokar in profile, placed to one side of the frame with open sea and Lovrijenac in the distance. Face north-west to look back at it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the fort on one side third of the frame, leaving the sea and Lovrijenac on the other. For an alternative, Pile Bay or Fort Lovrijenac shows Bokar's rounded seaward side rising from the rocks across the inlet. The exact stand point there is not fixed, so check the map.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fort to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or sea is washing out. Take a few frames, since people pass along the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the wall is generally quieter.

text.access_note: The wall-walk viewpoint needs a ticket, and entry rules for Fort Lovrijenac may apply too, so check the official site before you go.

name: Dubrovnik Bell Tower
label: Bell Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stradun' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Stradun nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/290668137: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gradski zvonik' (12 m across).
notes: The 31 m tower at the end of Stradun on Luža Square.

text.description: Dubrovnik's Bell Tower stands on Luža Square at the end of Stradun, the Old Town's main street. It is 31 metres high, with a clock face and a dome. That makes it a natural full stop for the long, straight view down the street, and this is the view the map points you to. The tower was first built in 1444. Over the centuries earthquakes damaged it, and by the early 19th century it had begun to lean towards Stradun. It was taken down in 1928 and rebuilt to the original design in 1929. The bronze bell that strikes the hours was cast in 1506. Two green-patinated bronze figures, known as Maro and Baro or the Zelenci, strike it. The ones on the tower now are replicas from 1929, and the originals from around 1478 are in the Cultural History Museum in the Rector's Palace. The stone street leads the eye straight to it, and people walking along it give the picture some scale. Take a few frames while you walk towards the tower. A wide shot along the street shows the whole scene, and a closer one picks out the clock face. If you want the bell strikers and the crowd below in one frame, Luža Square is a good second stop.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of Dubrovnik's Old Town, on Luža Square at the eastern end of Stradun, the main street.
text.directions_text: There are no listed stations or tram stops nearby, so begin from the Old Town itself. From there the tower is about 278 m on foot to the south-east, at the far end of the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the whole length of the street with the tower at the end. Then try 2x or more, if your phone has a telephoto lens, for a tighter shot of the tower and clock face. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and the building fronts on either side, and keep the tower in the middle of the frame so it does not look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Stradun (eastern end, standing on the street and looking back toward the tower from the Pile Gate direction). The tower closes the long perspective of the main street, with its clock face and dome centered at the end of the pedestrian walkway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on the central vertical line, with the street's edges leading towards it. Keep your phone level so the tower and the buildings do not lean. Wait for a gap in the crowd, or use the people as scale. For a different angle, Luža Square shows the clock face, the bronze strikers and the people below in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the clock face stays clear. Take a Live Photo if you like, since it may catch the movement in the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the street is less crowded.

text.access_note: Stradun is an open public street. Whether the tower itself can be climbed is unclear, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Pile Gate is at the western end of Stradun and is a usual place for visitors to enter the Old Town.
Stradun is a pedestrian street with a stone surface.
